title: What Breakthroughs Are Made Of
author: Cindy Chance
summary: Executive coach Cindy Chance argues that breakthroughs in coaching cannot be engineered, but they become likely inside a relationship of trust. She opens with the familiar scene of a child who says the important thing from the back seat of the car once the interrogation stops. Adults behave the same way: a guarded truth slips past an internal sensor during an unrelated story, a joke, or talk of a hobby. The sensor protects the ego, the managed self-image, and tender places, and it relaxes only when the other person is genuinely curious and safe. She cites a 2020 meta-analysis of 27 studies and over 3,500 coaching relationships showing that the strength of the working alliance, not session count or coach experience, predicted client gains. The practical lesson for any leader or coach is to coach the person rather than the problem and to invest in relational quality over time spent.
points: Breakthroughs tend to surface sideways, during an unguarded moment or an unrelated topic, rather than in response to direct questioning.
The internal sensor guards the ego and tender places, and it lowers only when the person feels safe, unpushed, and met with real curiosity.
A 2020 meta-analysis of 27 coaching studies found that working alliance strength predicted client outcomes, regardless of the number of sessions or the coach's experience.
Trust in coaching comes from competence, caring, integrity, and eliciting the client's agency, so quality of relationship matters more than quantity of time.
When the shift comes, the coach cannot plan it and must simply notice it and respond with presence and curiosity.
quotes: If you are a parent or ever cared for young children, you know that feeling of picking your child up and having a perfectly dull conversation.
It is as though a part of the person had been guarding a truth and the truth suddenly sneaked by the sensor.

As I think of examples from my work, it is striking how many times insights happen when a subject sneaks in, gets past the sensor because of a distraction or a joke or a moment that seems absolutely free and unrelated to the central issue of the coaching.
The sensor is guarding the ego, the well-managed self-image, and tender places.

In coaching, trust arises from the quality of the working relationship: how much competence, caring, and integrity are evidenced, and how much client agency is elicited. Time together is not the important factor; quality is.
A 2020 review of 27 coaching studies, covering more than 3,500 coaching relationships, found that the strength of the working alliance was closely linked to how much clients gained.
We cannot make a breakthrough happen. But remarkable clarity becomes possible, even likely, in the context of a trusting relationship.
